introduction: Mark Antony's love for Cleopatra places the pleasures and sovereignty of Egypt beside the demands of Roman rule. He shares imperial power with Octavius Caesar and Lepidus, but military threats and mistrust repeatedly pull him away from Alexandria. Cleopatra fears that political necessity will make affection disposable, while Antony struggles to reconcile his soldier's reputation with his devotion to her. Moving rapidly between courts, councils and battlefields, the tragedy follows the intimate costs of alliances made in pursuit of command over the world.

fullSynopsis.text: Mark Antony shares Roman power with Octavius Caesar and Lepidus, but his life with Cleopatra in Alexandria provokes Roman complaints that love has displaced his duties. News of rebellion involving his wife Fulvia, Parthian advances and the growing naval strength of Sextus Pompeius recalls him to public business. Fulvia's death makes Antony question the pleasures that have kept him away. Antony tells Cleopatra that necessity requires his departure while his heart remains hers; she alternates accusations, grief and affectionate farewell, then sends constant messages after him.

In Rome, Antony and Caesar exchange grievances before agreeing to reconcile through Antony's marriage to Caesar's sister Octavia. Enobarbus, Antony's companion, vividly recalls Cleopatra's hold over him and predicts that the marriage cannot sever it. A soothsayer warns Antony that Caesar's fortune overwhelms his own; Antony privately resolves to return east. Cleopatra violently receives news of the wedding. Meanwhile, the triumvirs negotiate peace with Pompey. At their drunken shipboard feast, Pompey refuses Menas's proposed murder of all three rivals, although he admits he would have welcomed the deed had it been done without consulting him.

The settlements unravel. While Ventidius wins in Parthia but avoids outshining his commander, Caesar renews war against Pompey and removes Lepidus. Antony sends Octavia to mediate with her brother, then rejoins Cleopatra. Caesar reports their public enthronement and distribution of kingdoms to her children, treating Antony's conduct as both political aggression and an insult to Octavia. Against his officers' advice, Antony accepts a sea battle at Actium. Cleopatra's ships flee, and he abandons the contest to follow her. Defections follow the defeat, though Enobarbus initially remains loyal.

Back in Alexandria, Antony reproaches Cleopatra but yields to her tears. Their ambassador asks Caesar for a reduced future for Antony and a royal inheritance for Cleopatra's children. Caesar rejects Antony's petition while encouraging Cleopatra to abandon or kill him. When Antony finds Caesar's envoy Thidias kissing her hand, he orders the messenger whipped and erupts in jealousy. Cleopatra reaffirms her devotion, and Antony regains the courage to fight. Enobarbus, however, sees renewed recklessness in his master's confidence and decides to desert.

Before battle, strange music leads soldiers to believe Antony's guardian Hercules is leaving him. Antony learns of Enobarbus's defection and sends his treasure after him with generous farewells. Enobarbus, overwhelmed by this kindness and his own betrayal, refuses to fight Antony. Antony wins a land engagement, briefly celebrating with Cleopatra and the wounded Scarus. That night Enobarbus dies lamenting him. On the next day his fleet goes over to Caesar. He interprets the surrender as Cleopatra's treachery and threatens her life, though her complicity is never established.

Cleopatra retreats to her monument and sends a false report that she has killed herself. Believing her dead, Antony commands Eros to kill him. Eros kills himself instead, and Antony follows his example but does not die immediately from his self-inflicted wound. Diomedes reveals that Cleopatra lives, and Antony is carried to her. She will not leave the monument for fear of capture, so she and her women haul him up. He dies with her after urging her to seek safety; she resolves to follow the Roman example of choosing death over subjection.

Caesar mourns Antony yet intends to display Cleopatra in his triumph. Proculeius captures her and prevents an immediate suicide; Dolabella later confirms Caesar's plan despite his promises of kindness. With her attendants Charmian and Iras, Cleopatra prepares a royal farewell. A countryman brings asps concealed with figs. Iras dies after their parting kisses; Cleopatra applies the snakes to her breast and arm, imagining reunion with Antony, and Charmian follows her. Arriving too late, Caesar acknowledges that Cleopatra has defeated his purpose and orders the lovers buried together with solemn military honours before he returns to Rome.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: In Alexandria, Antony's officers complain that his absorption in Cleopatra has transformed a great commander into a negligent lover. Antony dismisses Roman business, but messengers bring news of Fulvia's war, Parthian expansion and then Fulvia's death. He recognizes the dangers of continued absence, especially the rising power of Sextus Pompeius, and orders a return to Rome. Cleopatra tests and reproaches him, first invoking his marriage and then reading his reaction to Fulvia's death as a warning of her own future. They nevertheless part with assurances of love. In Rome, Caesar criticizes Antony's pleasures while recalling his former endurance as a soldier; Pompey's sea power makes military preparation urgent. Left in Egypt, Cleopatra longs for Antony, treasures his messages and arranges a constant stream of her own.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Pompey hopes the triumvirs' divisions will aid him but fears Antony's return. In Rome, Lepidus mediates between Antony and Caesar, whose grievances include Antony's neglect of promised assistance. Agrippa proposes marriage to Octavia as a lasting bond, and both rulers consent. Enobarbus describes Cleopatra's magnificent first meeting with Antony and doubts that he can leave her. A soothsayer warns that Caesar's fortune surpasses Antony's; Antony decides his pleasure lies in Egypt, despite the marriage made for peace. Cleopatra strikes and threatens the messenger who reports the wedding, then demands details of her rival. At Misenum, Pompey accepts Sicily and Sardinia in return for clearing pirates and supplying Rome with grain. During the celebratory feast aboard his galley, Menas offers to murder the three rulers. Pompey refuses to authorize it, and Menas privately resolves to leave his service.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Ventidius defeats the Parthians but limits his success to avoid provoking Antony's jealousy. As Antony and Octavia leave Rome, Caesar warns that their marriage must be cherished if it is to preserve peace. Cleopatra finds comfort in a messenger's disparaging description of Octavia. In Athens, Antony accuses Caesar of renewing war against Pompey and belittling him; Octavia departs to mediate. News follows of Lepidus's imprisonment and Pompey's murder. Caesar reports Antony's return to Cleopatra and their public grants of kingdoms to her children, presenting Octavia as abandoned. At Actium, Antony insists on fighting by sea despite his land advantage. Cleopatra's flight draws him after her, and officers prepare to surrender. In Alexandria he forgives her, while Caesar rejects his requests and courts her separately. Antony has Thidias whipped for kissing her hand, then accepts her assurances and prepares to fight again. Enobarbus decides that loyalty has become folly.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Caesar dismisses Antony's challenge to single combat and plans battle. Antony's emotional farewell to his servants unsettles them; night watchmen interpret mysterious music as Hercules abandoning him. Cleopatra helps arm Antony before he learns that Enobarbus has deserted. He sends the deserter his treasure and good wishes, a generosity that makes Enobarbus condemn himself. Antony and Scarus win a land victory; that night Enobarbus dies in remorse. The following naval action ends when Antony's fleet joins Caesar. Antony blames Cleopatra, threatening revenge without proof that she arranged the betrayal. She hides in her monument and orders Mardian to announce her suicide. Believing her dead, Antony asks Eros to kill him; Eros kills himself instead. Antony falls on his own sword but remains alive. Diomedes corrects the false report, and attendants carry Antony to the monument. Cleopatra and her women draw him up rather than risk capture below. Antony dies with her, and she resolves to choose death herself.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Dercetus brings Antony's bloody sword to Caesar, who mourns his former partner while preparing to secure Cleopatra for his Roman triumph. Proculeius reassures her, then helps capture and disarm her. Cleopatra rejects the prospect of public humiliation and remembers Antony in language that makes him larger than the world. Dolabella confirms that Caesar will display her in triumph. Caesar promises gentleness but warns that suicide would endanger her children; after her treasurer reveals concealed wealth, he allows her to keep it. Cleopatra sees persuasion in his kindness and prepares her own end. A countryman supplies asps in a basket of figs. Dressed in crown and robe, she kisses her women goodbye; Iras dies, then Cleopatra and Charmian use the snakes. Caesar finds them dead, recognizes that his intended spectacle is lost and orders Cleopatra buried beside Antony with a solemn funeral.
